payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=methods+for+evaluating+problem+significance+or+interestingness+in+autonomous+scientific+discovery+agents+without+human+labels&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.5907404\", \"title\": [\"Financial Autonomous AI Agents: Buying Services and Data without Human Intervention\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5907404\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"title\": [\"A Brief History of AI for Scientific Discovery: Open Research, Metrics, and Autonomous Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The history of artificial intelligence for scientific discovery is not a two year story about chatbots learning to write papers. It is a sixty year story about science repeatedly handing its bottlenecks to machines—first inference, then search, then measurement, then the full workflow—only to discover that each delegation solves one problem and exposes a harder one underneath. This paper traces that history from DENDRAL (1965) through the construction of open scholarly infrastructure (arXiv, Google Scholar, ORCID), the oracle breakthroughs of AlphaFold, and the current era of LLM driven autonomous research agents. Three interlocking threads are followed including AI as research instrument, AI for research infrastructure, and the reshaping of scholarly profiles and incentives by machine readable metrics. The central tension throughout is between automation and augmentation between building systems that replace human researchers and tools that amplify human creativity and judgement. The paper presents that the most consequential development is not any single tool but the emergence of an interconnected ecosystem where AI agents, preprint platforms, open source codebases, and citation infrastructure form a feedback loop that is fundamentally restructuring who can do science, how fast discoveries propagate, and what counts as a valid scientific contribution.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 3, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/11564126_45\", \"title\": [\"Evaluating the Correlation Between Objective Rule Interestingness Measures and Real Human Interest\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/11564126_45\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2005]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/axlh3545\", \"title\": [\"AI for Advancing Scientific Discovery for a Sustainable Future\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a rapidly advancing field. Novel machine learning methods combined with reasoning and search techniques have led us to reach new milestones: from computer vision, machine translation, and Go and Chess world-champion level play using pure self-training strategies, to self-driving cars. These ever-expanding AI capabilities open up new exciting avenues for advances in new domains. I will discuss our AI research for advancing scientific discovery for a sustainable future. In particular, I will talk about our research in a new interdisciplinary field, Computational Sustainability, which has the overarching goal of developing computational models and methods to help manage the balance between environmental, economic, and societal needs for a sustainable future. I will provide examples of computational sustainability problems, ranging from biodiversity and wildlife conservation, to multi-criteria strategic planning of hydropower dams in the Amazon basin and materials discovery for renewable energy materials. I will also highlight cross-cutting computational themes and challenges for AI at the intersection of constraint reasoning, optimization, machine learning, multi-agent reasoning, citizen science, and crowd-sourcing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/axlh3545\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2020, 5, 5]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "23fc0be3be136f15970f8b479fa49d6cd3f16060f2b6beaf666b095971d9032f", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.5907404", "doi:10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1", "doi:10.1007/11564126_45", "doi:10.65109/axlh3545"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5907404", "https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1", "https://doi.org/10.1007/11564126_45", "https://doi.org/10.65109/axlh3545"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

actions.body: Research into autonomous systems reveals a critical distinction between executing assigned tasks and formulating new ones. Systems equipped with self-generated goal mechanisms—like those explored in the GOAL-Robots paradigm—demonstrate significant advantages in skill acquisition, particularly under unpredictable conditions. However, the path to independent scientific discovery is iterative and non-linear. Collected evidence highlights that autonomous agents frequently encounter failure loops when addressing complex, multi-file scientific challenges. Consequently, robustness in autonomous research hinges on 'self-healing' capabilities—the ability to identify failures, adapt hypotheses, and recover partial progress without external guidance. Furthermore, moving beyond random exploration requires meta-strategies that prioritize empirical accountability, ensuring that an agent's self-selected research direction yields meaningful, rather than merely novel, results. The synthesis of goal generation, failure recovery, and strategic prioritization constitutes the architecture of true autonomous scientific inquiry.
actions.lede: Autonomous inquiry is not merely the execution of assigned tasks; it requires active goal generation and self-healing in the face of failure.
